Thursday, 13 February 2031, 3 a.m. Henri-Ion is six weeks old and won’t sleep. Julien is walking him round the living room. Ioana wakes up and comes into the kitchen.
What’s wrong with him? I just heard him crying.
Nothing. He’s just finished his bottle. He’s digesting. And I’m going mad.
Give him to me. You’re about to fall asleep on your feet.
No, wait. Look: he’s about to close his eyes. If I stop now, he’ll start crying again.
Since he was born, you haven’t slept a whole night.
Neither have you. But as long as he needs me, I’ll stay up. And besides, I’m starting to like these nights. You can hear the city breathing.
You say that now. In three weeks you start travelling again. Now that the plantings are starting again, you won’t have the time.
I asked Amina to organise everything so that I’m never away more than one night. As he grows, I’ll go away a bit more.
So you finally talked to her? She lets you take breaks?
She began by refusing. Then she made a spreadsheet. In the end she sent me a schedule entitled “Paternity”. In colour.
(laughs softly) Shh… Look. He’s falling asleep. For real, this time.
(very quietly) Don’t move. Don’t breathe. As we talk, his eyes are closing.

French has precise expressions for each moment of an action. Imagine a timeline:
être sur le point de + inf.
Il est sur le point de s’endormir.
Il est en train de s’endormir.
“Être en train de” stresses that the action is happening RIGHT NOW. English uses the progressive (“he’s falling asleep”), which French doesn’t have as a tense.
Don’t confuse “finir de” (to finish doing something) with “finir par” (to end up doing): “Il a fini de manger” (he finished eating) ≠ “Il a fini par manger” (he eventually ate).
In the past, these expressions go into the IMPERFECT, because they describe a situation:
I was sleeping when he cried.
I had just fallen asleep when he woke up.
I was about to leave when she called.
“Je venais de” (imperfect) = I had just… Don’t say “je suis venu de” ✗ — that means “I came from (a place)”.

À mesure qu’il grandit, il dort mieux.

Au fur et à mesure qu’on parle, ses yeux se ferment.
After “tant que” with future meaning, use the FUTURE: “Tant qu’il aura besoin de moi, je resterai.” (not the present, as in English).

Henri-Ion’s first weeks of life were a succession of sleepless nights, bottles and lullabies. Julien had started keeping a little night diary, which he wrote with one hand while rocking his son with the other. Ioana said it was the only diary in the world where every page began with a time in the middle of the night.

Elena had gone back to Iași at the end of January, crying at the airport as if she were leaving for ever. She had left behind a freezer full of sarmale, soups and cakes, and a list of twenty-seven tips stuck on the fridge. Tip number one was: “Sleep when the baby sleeps.” Nobody had managed to follow it.

Since Elena’s departure, Odile had been coming to help in the afternoons. She now walked with a stick, slowly, stopping in the middle of the landing to catch her breath. But she came every day, at three o’clock sharp, and sat in the armchair by the window with Henri-Ion in her arms while Ioana slept for an hour.

During that hour, Odile talked to the baby. Nobody knew exactly what she told him. One day Ioana, waking earlier than planned, heard a few sentences from the bedroom. Odile was telling him about the sea, distant ports, a sailor who whistled on the deck of a ship. She spoke to him the way you speak to someone you find again after a long absence.

Rose-Hélène had taken a few weeks to accept her little brother. At first she looked at him warily, like an intruder who had stolen the whole family’s attention. She started talking like a baby, asking for a bottle, refusing to walk. Then, one February morning, she discovered she had a power nobody else had.

Henri-Ion had been crying for an hour. Julien had tried everything: the bottle, the dummy, the walk up and down the corridor, the lullaby. Nothing worked. Then Rose-Hélène went up to the cot with Henri’s harmonica and blew the first three notes of the waltz. Her little brother stopped crying at once and turned his head towards her.

From that day on, Rose-Hélène declared herself officially in charge of her brother’s calm. As soon as he started crying, she came running with her harmonica. She took her role very seriously. She even demanded to be called when he cried at night. Julien negotiated: only before nine in the evening. She finally agreed, with a sigh.

On 4 March 2031 Rose-Hélène turned three. There was no big party this time, just a chocolate cake, three candles and the family. While she was blowing out the candles, Henri-Ion, in his mother’s arms, smiled. It was his first real smile. Rose-Hélène decided it was for her. Nobody dared say otherwise.

On Monday 10 March, Julien went back to work full time. Amina was waiting for him at the Croix-Rousse office with a coffee, a pile of files and the famous “Paternity” schedule, printed in colour and pinned on the wall. Each trip was limited to one night. The spring plantings had been organised so that Julien would always be home before Henri-Ion woke for his six o’clock bottle.

The first planting took place in Toulouse on Saturday 15 March, in the Mirail district. It was fine and mild, real spring weather. The Toulouse orchestra, created in September, already had forty children. They played the waltz under the plane trees, in front of a school, and a little eight-year-old violinist played the opening solo with impressive concentration.

Odile attended the planting by video, from her armchair on rue d’Austerlitz, with Henri-Ion on her lap. She checked the label, as always. Then, at the third verse, she whistled her part, and the Toulouse children, who had been told, stopped to listen to her. Her voice was weak, but it could be heard clearly through the speaker.

A week later, on Saturday 22 March, it was Nantes’ turn. The city had chosen as its rehearsal hall a former shipyard shed on the banks of the Loire, where ships had been built for more than a century. The lime tree would be planted on the quay, between two old yellow cranes. Julien found the spot perfect. Henri would have liked to sleep next to a shipyard.

The ceremony was simple. The deputy mayor said a few words. The children of the Nantes orchestra played the waltz, accompanied by an old ship’s siren that an enthusiast had got working again for the occasion. Julien planted the tree with two children, and Odile, on Amina’s tablet, whistled the third verse from Lyon.

After the ceremony, an old man came up to Julien. He must have been over eighty. He wore a sailor’s cap and a navy pea jacket worn threadbare, and he walked with difficulty, leaning on a carved wooden stick. He had waited until everyone had left. Then he asked, in a hoarse voice: “The lady on the screen. Is she really Henri Bernard’s wife?”

Julien froze. The man’s name was Yves Le Goff. He was eighty-seven. He had sailed with Henri on the same cargo ship for six years in the seventies. Together they had done Africa, South America, the Indian Ocean. “He whistled that tune every evening on deck,” Yves said. “Every evening. We used to tease him. We called him the whistler.”

Yves had read in the local paper that a lime tree linked to a sailor’s story would be planted on the quay. He had recognised the name. He had come, just in case. And when he heard the children play the waltz, then the lady whistling on the screen, he had to sit down on a bench, because his legs wouldn’t hold him. He hadn’t heard it for fifty years.

Yves also told them something nobody knew. Henri couldn’t play the piano any more, because of the two fingers he had lost in Algeria. That was why he had learned the harmonica, on the ship, during the long night watches. “He said it was the only instrument you can play with a hand and a half,” Yves explained. “He hid it in his left pocket, with his injured hand. He didn’t want anyone to see him play.”

Then he rummaged in the pocket of his pea jacket and took out a small rectangular plastic object, yellowed with age. It was an audio cassette. On the label, handwritten in almost faded ink, it read: “Henri, harmonica, Dakar, 1978”. Julien looked at the cassette without understanding.

“I had a little tape recorder on the ship,” Yves explained. “One evening in Dakar, during a stopover, I recorded Henri without him knowing. He was playing the harmonica on deck. He was playing your waltz. When he found out, he got angry. He asked me to erase the tape. I never did. I’ve kept it for fifty-three years.”

He held the cassette out to Julien. “It’s for her. For the lady. I have no family left, and I don’t know how much time I have. I wanted it to go to someone who knows what it’s worth.” Julien took the cassette in his hands, as carefully as if he were holding the baby. He couldn’t manage to say anything but thank you.

On the train home, Julien didn’t let go of the cassette. Amina, sitting opposite him, spent the whole journey searching on her phone for where you could still find a cassette player in 2031. “It’s like looking for a dinosaur,” she sighed. Then she looked up. “Do you realise, Mr Moreau? Nobody has ever heard Henri play. Except Odile.”

At the office on Monday morning, Julien told Amina the whole story in detail. She listened without interrupting, which never happened. At the end, she opened a new document on her computer. Julien expected a spreadsheet. It was a letter addressed to Yves Le Goff, officially inviting him to the Lyon planting next spring, at the ministry’s expense. “It isn’t an emotion,” she specified. “It’s an invitation.”

It was Radu who found the solution. In the cellar of the office building, among the old furniture left by former tenants, there was an old radio-cassette player from the nineties, covered in dust. Radu cleaned it, changed the batteries, and tried it with an old cassette of French songs found in the same box. It worked. A little slowly, but it worked.

On Sunday 23 March, late in the afternoon, they all gathered at Odile’s. Ioana, Julien, the two children, Radu, Lucia, and Isabelle, who had come from Paris as soon as she heard the news. Julien hadn’t told Odile anything. He just asked her to sit in her armchair by the window. Then he put the old radio-cassette player on the little table in front of her.

He told her about Nantes, the quay, the yellow cranes and the old sailor in the cap. When he said the name Yves Le Goff, Odile put her hand to her mouth. “Yves,” she murmured. “The Breton. Henri talked about him all the time. He said he was the only one on board who could cook.” Julien took the cassette out of his pocket and showed it to her.

Odile read the label. “Henri, harmonica, Dakar, 1978.” She said nothing. Her hands began to tremble. Julien put the cassette into the machine and pressed the button. First there was a long hiss, a crackle, the distant sound of the sea against a hull, men’s voices laughing in the background. Then, suddenly, a harmonica.

It was the waltz. The first three notes, then the rest, played slowly, slightly out of tune at times, with a breath you could hear between the phrases. It wasn’t perfect. It was better than perfect. It was a man alone on the deck of a ship, off the coast of Africa, in 1978, playing for a woman he hadn’t seen for sixteen years and would never see again.

Odile closed her eyes. Tears ran down her cheeks, silently. Isabelle knelt beside the armchair and took her mother’s hand. She was crying too. She had never heard her father play that instrument. She only knew he had one, that he kept it in a drawer and never took it out when anyone was watching.

Rose-Hélène, sitting on the floor, listened with total attention. Then she took Henri’s harmonica out of her pocket, the real one, the one that had been used for the recording fifty-three years earlier. And when the waltz reached the third verse on the tape, she blew her three notes at the same time as the harmonica of 1978. The same instrument, half a century apart, was playing with itself.

When the music stopped there was a long silence, filled only by the hiss of the tape. Then, on the cassette, a man’s voice, young, a little annoyed, said: “Yves, turn that thing off, I saw you.” And a burst of laughter. Then nothing more. Odile opened her eyes again. “That’s him,” she said. “That’s his voice. He was thirty-eight.”

That evening Odile asked for copies of the cassette to be made. One for Isabelle. One for the Hélène Morel hall, so that the La Duchère children could hear the man who had written their waltz. One for Yves Le Goff, to whom she wanted to write a long letter. And a last one, which she asked to be put in the envelope Rose-Hélène would open on her twentieth birthday.

Radu digitised the recording during the night, at his office, cleaning up the sound as best he could without erasing the sound of the sea. He felt the sea was part of the music. The next morning, when Julien arrived at the Croix-Rousse, Amina had already put the file on a USB stick, with a typed label: “Henri Bernard, harmonica, Dakar, 1978. National archive of the network.”

The following Monday, Julien took a copy of the recording to the Parc de la Tête d’Or. He found Mr Fournier in the greenhouse, repotting the last lime trees. They walked together to the old tree with the carved letters. Julien put his phone on the bench and played the recording. The gardener listened, hat in hand, without a word.

When the music had died away, he put his hand on the bark, right next to the two H’s. “Sixty-nine years this one has been waiting to hear that,” he said. “Trees have memory, you know. More than we do.” Then he went back to his pots without adding anything. Julien saw him wipe his eyes with the back of his sleeve, pretending to brush off some soil.

On Saturday 5 April, in Clermont-Ferrand, the sixty-three children who had written the letter to the mayor planted their lime tree in front of the old school, converted into a rehearsal hall. Mr Benhamou had sent from Marseille, by post, an olive post to serve as a stake, with a note: “In case the Auvergne wind is jealous of the mistral.” It wasn’t. The weather was magnificent.

Before playing the waltz, Julien did something he had never done. He put a small speaker on a chair in front of the children and played them the Dakar recording. The sound of the sea, the breathing, the slightly out-of-tune harmonica, the annoyed voice at the end. The children listened in silence, mouths open. Then a little girl raised her hand.

“Sir, is that him? The sailor?” Julien nodded. “And he played out of tune?” Julien smiled. “A little.” The little girl thought, then announced to the whole class, very pleased: “Then we’re allowed to as well.” The sixty-three children burst out laughing, and played the waltz more freely than ever, with wrong notes and lots of joy.

Back in Lyon, Julien found a letter on the kitchen table. It came from Nantes. It was Yves Le Goff answering Odile’s letter. He had written three pages in a shaky hand, full of memories: storms, stopovers, evenings on deck. At the end he had added a sentence for Julien: “Thank you for having his waltz played by children. He would have pretended to be angry. But he would have been very proud.”

That evening, before going to bed, Odile listened to the cassette one last time, alone, in her sitting room. Julien heard her through the door: the sound of the sea, the harmonica, Henri’s voice. Then silence. Then, after a long while, Odile whistling, very softly, the third verse. She was whistling with him. For the first time in eight years, they were playing together.

Ten past three. He’s just woken up for the second time. Ioana is finally asleep. I picked him up before he could really start crying. I’m writing with one hand while rocking him with the other.
Since he was born, I’ve discovered a city I didn’t know: Lyon at three in the morning. The last tram, the dustbin lorry, a cat on the roof opposite. And the silence, which is never complete.

As the weeks go by, he changes. He’s starting to follow light with his eyes. He finally accepted the dummy, after refusing it for a month. And when Rose-Hélène plays the harmonica, he stops crying immediately.
Twenty to four. He was about to fall asleep when a motorbike went past in the street. Back to square one. I hum the waltz to him, as on the night he was born. As I sing, he calms down.
Across the landing, I saw the light come on at Odile’s. She doesn’t sleep much any more either. As long as she’s there, on the other side of that door, I think the waltz will never stop.

Four o’clock. He’s asleep. I don’t dare move. I’m going to stay here, sitting in the dark, with my son on my chest, until day breaks. Now that I think about it, these may be the most beautiful hours of my life.
